subtype: Friend × Recognising a toxic pattern from outside [Actor]
passage:
Dear Ramesh,
I have been thinking about how to say this, so I will say it once and then leave it. Over the last few months you have stopped coming to cricket, you check your phone before answering me, and last week you looked frightened when a call came in. I might be wrong. I am not telling you what to do, and I am not asking you to choose between us. I just want you to know what I have noticed, and that I am on your side either way. I will keep saving your seat in the canteen. If you want to talk, or just sit quietly, call me any time, day or night, and I will not ask questions.
Your friend,
Jatin

qa.q: What has Jatin noticed about Ramesh over the last few months?
qa.a: Jatin noticed that Ramesh stopped coming to cricket, checks the phone before answering, and looked frightened when a call came in.

qa.q: What is Jatin worried about, and how can you tell from the careful wording?
qa.a: Jatin worries about Ramesh but does not want Ramesh to feel judged or cornered. Writing "I might be wrong" and "I am not asking you to choose" shows care for the friendship and a wish to keep the door open.

qa.q: What could Jatin do after sending the letter?
qa.a: Jatin can keep the seat saved, stay in touch in ordinary ways, listen without judging, and not repeat the warning or give ultimatums.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Ramesh may feel worried, exposed or defensive at first, but also relieved that there is no pressure. Ramesh also learns someone is ready to listen at any hour.

grounding: A friend sees a controlling relationship from outside, shares the concern once, and keeps the door open without ultimatums.

subtype: Friend × Recognising a toxic pattern from outside [Actor]
passage:
June: Madhuri noticed Deepak checking his phone every few minutes at their café table and leaving early because Vani 'needed to know where he was'. She wanted to say, 'Just dump her.' Instead she asked, 'How are things with you two?' and listened.
July: Deepak cancelled three plans in a row. Madhuri sent a voice note anyway: 'No pressure. I'm around Saturday if you want samosas.' He came, quieter than usual.
August: Over samosas, Madhuri said it once, gently: 'From outside, it looks like Vani decides a lot of your time. I could be wrong. I just don't want you to feel alone in it.' Deepak went stiff and changed the subject. Madhuri let it go and said, 'Saturday stands, every week.' Two weeks later he texted: 'Can we talk? About Vani.'

qa.q: What did Madhuri offer in the July voice note?
qa.a: Madhuri said, 'I'm around Saturday if you want samosas.'

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling in June when Deepak left early?
qa.a: Madhuri felt worried and frustrated, tempted to tell Deepak to end it, but chose to listen instead.

qa.q: What went right in how Madhuri raised her concern in August?
qa.a: Madhuri said it once, gently, admitted she could be wrong and kept Saturday open, so Deepak always had a way back.

qa.q: What would change for Deepak if Madhuri had given him an ultimatum?
qa.a: Deepak might have felt judged and pulled closer to Vani, and the 'Can we talk?' text may never have come.

grounding: Shows a friend who sees a controlling relationship from outside, stays close, listens, voices the concern once and keeps the door open.

subtype: Friend × Recognising a toxic pattern from outside [Actor]
passage: Rafiq, you're asking what to do about your friend. Let your Rekha-aunty tell you about Shobha. We were twenty, sharing a room in a working women's hostel in Pune. Her fiancé phoned every hour and decided what she wore. One night I lost my temper: 'Either you leave him, or never talk to me about him again.' She never talked to me about him again. For four months she didn't talk to me at all. That silence frightened me more than he did. So I swallowed my pride and left a tiffin of her favourite poha outside her door with a note: 'No speeches. Just miss you.' She came back slowly. I listened, mostly. Once, only once, I told her what I saw. A year later she was the one who asked me to help her pack.

qa.q: Where did Rekha and Shobha share a room?
qa.a: They shared a room in a working women's hostel in Pune.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling during the four months of silence?
qa.a: Rekha felt frightened and regretful, afraid the ultimatum had cut Shobha off from someone who could help.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things between Rekha and Shobha?
qa.a: Leaving the poha tiffin with a 'No speeches' note, then mostly listening and saying what she saw only once.

qa.q: How might Shobha have felt when she was given the ultimatum?
qa.a: Shobha likely felt judged and cornered, so she shut Rekha out rather than choose, and only later felt safe enough to ask for help.

grounding: An aunt recalls how an ultimatum pushed a friend in a controlling engagement away, and how staying close, listening and speaking once kept the door open.
